[PATH:empirical] World Bank Data on Aid Effectiveness and Governance Indicators (e.g., Worldwide Governance Indicators, CPIA) combined with GDP growth data from low-income countries post-2000 — This source allows a quantitative test of the hypothesis by correlating foreign aid inflows with economic growth specifically in countries that score high on governance and financial transparency measures, controlling for other growth determinants.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review or meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials and quasi-experimental studies on aid-funded projects in transparent governance contexts (e.g., from 3ie, AidData, or published in journals like Journal of Development Economics) — A synthesis of existing causal evidence can confirm or refute the conditional effect, aggregating findings across multiple settings to assess whether strong governance amplifies aid's growth impact.

C006.subject: foreign aid
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: foreign aid in countries with strong governance]

[PATH:empirical] World Bank Independent Evaluation Group (IEG) reports on aid effectiveness in Sub-Saharan Africa and Southeast Asia (2000-2020) — Provides quantitative data on GDP growth, institutional capacity, and dependency measures in strong-governance countries, enabling direct test of the hypothesis.

[PATH:literature] Bourguignon & Sundberg (2007) 'Aid Effectiveness: Opening the Black Box' (American Economic Review) — Reviews theoretical mechanisms and empirical evidence on how aid interacts with governance quality, offering a foundational critique of the dependency claim.

[PATH:empirical] Regression discontinuity designs using aid allocation thresholds in well-governed districts (e.g., from AidData or ODI research) — Allows causal identification of aid's effect on economic autonomy vs. dependency, controlling for selection bias in strong-governance contexts.

C007.subject: foreign aid
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: foreign aid in recipient countries]

[PATH:empirical] World Bank Development Indicators and AidData research datasets (e.g., AidData's Geocoded Global Aid Data) for sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, post-2000 — These datasets allow panel regressions linking sectoral aid flows (e.g., infrastructure, agriculture, education) to changes in the Herfindahl-Hirschman Index of export or production concentration, directly testing whether aid correlates with diversification over time and across countries.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis or systematic review of existing econometric studies on foreign aid and economic diversification (e.g., in Journal of Development Economics or World Development) — A synthesis of published findings can reveal overall effect sizes, heterogeneity by region or aid type, and methodological biases, helping to resolve the disputed status of the hypothesis with higher statistical power.

[PATH:empirical] Case-study analysis of specific aid programs (e.g., USAID's 'Feed the Future' or DFID's 'Growth and Diversification' initiatives) in countries like Ghana, Bangladesh, or Ethiopia, using difference-in-differences or synthetic control methods — Program-level quasi-experimental designs can isolate causal effects of targeted aid on sectoral diversification indicators, addressing endogeneity concerns that plague cross-country regressions.

C008.subject: foreign aid
C008.predicate: enables investment in local capacity and infrastructure that reduces long-term dependency
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: foreign aid in recipient countries]

[PATH:empirical] A systematic review of World Bank project evaluations in Sub-Saharan Africa (2000-2020) focusing on infrastructure and capacity-building outcomes — World Bank evaluation reports provide standardized, longitudinal data on project-level impacts of foreign aid on local infrastructure and capacity, enabling direct testing of whether such investments reduce dependency over time.

[PATH:empirical] Comparative case studies of aid-dependent vs. aid-independent countries in Sub-Saharan Africa using difference-in-differences or synthetic control methods — This research design can isolate the causal effect of sustained foreign aid on economic self-sufficiency by comparing trajectories of countries that received large aid inflows with those that did not, controlling for confounding factors.

[PATH:literature] Theoretical literature on the 'aid dependency trap' vs. 'catalytic aid' models (e.g., Sachs vs. Easterly debates, updated with post-2000 evidence) — A targeted review of competing theoretical frameworks and their empirical tests in Sub-Saharan Africa can clarify the conditions under which aid enables versus undermines local capacity, refining the hypothesis's scope conditions.

C011.subject: foreign aid
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: foreign aid when combined with infrastructure development]

[PATH:empirical] World Bank Independent Evaluation Group reports on aid effectiveness and infrastructure projects in low-income countries since 2000 — Provides systematic impact evaluations and cost-benefit analyses of aid programs that bundle infrastructure with other interventions, allowing comparison with aid without infrastructure components.

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) from the Abdul Latif Jameel Poverty Action Lab (J-PAL) examining combined infrastructure and cash transfer programs in sub-Saharan Africa — RCTs offer high internal validity to isolate the causal effect of the infrastructure-aid combination on poverty reduction, controlling for confounding factors.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis by the International Initiative for Impact Evaluation (3ie) on the synergies between infrastructure investment and foreign aid in poverty alleviation — Synthesizes multiple studies to assess whether the interaction effect is consistently positive across contexts, addressing publication bias and heterogeneity.

C012.subject: foreign aid
C012.object: more effectively when directed to infrastructure and governance reform, not health and education
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: foreign aid more effectively when directed to infrastructure and governance reform, not health and education]

[PATH:empirical] A meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials and quasi-experimental studies on foreign aid effectiveness in sub-Saharan Africa, comparing outcomes of infrastructure/governance aid vs. health/education aid on poverty measures (e.g., income, asset indices) since 2000. — Directly tests the comparative poverty reduction impact of different aid categories using rigorous causal methods, addressing the core hypothesis with region and time scope matched.

[PATH:empirical] Panel data regression analysis using World Bank and OECD aid data (e.g., CRS) combined with national poverty statistics (e.g., World Bank PovcalNet) for sub-Saharan African countries from 2000 to present, controlling for initial conditions and governance quality. — Provides macro-level evidence on the relationship between aid composition and poverty trends over time, allowing for assessment of generalizable patterns and potential confounding factors.

[PATH:theoretical] Theoretical and empirical literature on public goods provision and institutional capacity (e.g., Acemoglu & Robinson, 2012; Collier, 2007) applied to aid allocation, arguing that infrastructure and governance reforms build state capacity and economic fundamentals, while direct health/education aid may have weaker long-term poverty effects due to fungibility and absorptive capacity constraints. — Offers a causal mechanism linking aid type to poverty reduction, which can be tested against the empirical evidence and helps interpret findings beyond correlation.
